items.stem: A row probability vector π is stationary for P when:
items.explanation: Stationarity means one transition leaves the row distribution unchanged.

items.stem: Which condition is part of the definition of a stationary distribution?
options: Every entry of P is equal
items.explanation: A stationary distribution must also be a probability vector.
The first coordinate gives 0.8x+0.4(1−x)=x, hence x=2/3.
items.check: The vector (2/3,1/3) is nonnegative, sums to one and is unchanged by multiplication.

items.stem: Under the row-vector convention, the distribution after one step from α is:
items.explanation: A row distribution is multiplied on the right by P.

items.stem: Which statements are true about a stationary distribution?
items.explanation: A, B and D are true; uniformity is not required.
statements: Its entries are nonnegative and sum to one.
If the chain starts with π, its distribution remains π.

A.why: This is the defining invariance equation.

B.why: A stationary distribution is a probability vector.

C.why: Stationary probabilities need not be equal.

D.why: Starting from π leaves the distribution unchanged after every transition, so πPⁿ=π for all n.

items.stem: A finite-state Markov chain is guaranteed to have:
options: a unique stationary distribution in every case
items.explanation: Every finite stochastic matrix has at least one stationary probability vector.

items.stem: For P=[[0.7,0.3],[0.2,0.8]], find the stationary probability of state 1.
items.explanation: Let π₁=x and π₂=1−x. The stationary equation for state 1 is x=0.7x+0.2(1−x), so 0.1x=0.2(1−x), giving x=2/5. The two stationary probabilities therefore sum to one.
items.check: The vector (2/5,3/5) is nonnegative, sums to one and is unchanged by P.

items.stem: For P=[[a,1−a],[b,1−b]], with b+1−a>0, the stationary probability of state 1 is:
items.explanation: The balance equation is x(1−a)=(1−x)b; solving gives x=b/(b+1−a).
For a two-state chain with transition probabilities a=P₁₂=0.4 and b=P₂₁=0.3, stationarity gives π₁a=π₂b. Normalising yields π₁=b/(a+b)=0.3/0.7=3/7.
items.check: Check that π₂=4/7 and the vector is unchanged by multiplication.

items.stem: For a finite irreducible chain, which statements are true?
items.explanation: A, B and C hold. Periodicity can prevent convergence despite uniqueness.
statements: If the chain is also aperiodic, distributions converge to it from every initial state.

A.why: Finite chains have a stationary distribution.

C.why: Aperiodicity together with finite irreducibility gives convergence.

items.explanation: The equations imply x=y=z; normalization gives each component 1/3.

items.stem: For a finite irreducible periodic chain, which statement is correct?
options: It must converge from every initial state
It has infinitely many stationary distributions
It has a unique stationary distribution, but convergence may fail
items.explanation: Finite irreducibility gives a unique stationary distribution; periodicity can cause oscillation.

items.stem: For P=I₂, which is the complete set of stationary distributions?
items.explanation: Every probability vector satisfies πI₂=π.

items.stem: Which equation is the normalization condition for π=(x,y,z)?
items.explanation: The probabilities assigned to all states must sum to one.

items.stem: If π is stationary, what is πPⁿ for any nonnegative integer n?
items.explanation: Stationarity means πP=π. Multiplying by P repeatedly gives πP²=(πP)P=πP=π, and induction yields πPⁿ=π for every nonnegative integer n.
Detailed balance gives π₂=2π₁ and π₃=3π₁/2. Normalizing gives (9/2)π₁=1, hence π₁=2/9.
items.check: Check: (2/9,4/9,1/3) sums to one and satisfies πP=π.

items.stem: For P=[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[1/3,1/3,1/3]], which describes all stationary distributions?
items.explanation: Solving πP=π forces the third component to zero; the first two can be any nonnegative pair summing to one.

items.stem: Consider P=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Which statement is true?
options: (1/2,1/2) is unique stationary, but starting at state 1 the distributions oscillate
items.explanation: The chain alternates deterministically. The equal vector is stationary, but a point-mass initial distribution alternates.

items.stem: Which statements correctly distinguish existence, uniqueness and convergence?
items.explanation: A, B and C are true; uniqueness does not alone imply convergence.
statements: Every finite chain has at least one stationary distribution.
A finite irreducible chain has a unique stationary distribution.
A finite irreducible aperiodic chain converges to its stationary distribution.
A unique stationary distribution alone guarantees convergence.

A.why: Finite stochastic matrices have a stationary probability vector.

D.why: Periodic irreducible chains can fail to converge.

items.stem: For P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.5,0.5]], what is the stationary probability of state 1?
items.explanation: Use π₁=b/(b+1−a)=0.5/(0.5+0.1)=5/6. The other probability is 1/6.
